claims.text: ADR 0026 header: not built at stage-4, no multi-shop code in the repository; the design and its review are in docs/design/multi-shop-design-review.md.

ADR 0026 chooses the second option: table shops (owned by Ordering, in donhang) gains a column recording the database holding the shop's data, default the shared database donhang; shared tables stay the default for every other shop.
From release 2 of multi-shop-data-rollout.md, each request takes its shop from the access token, looks up that shop's database in the map, then opens a connection there.
Each Pod keeps the map in memory for a short time, 30 seconds (assumed).
Only DonHang.Api's database (donhang) moves shops out; Notifications and Payments keep every shop in shared tables because each shop's data there is small.

The map is a dependency of every request: unreadable means no request knows its database (ADR consequences); the in-Pod cache lets requests run on for up to 30 seconds, after which new requests stop; the review calls the map a new single point of failure.

Moving a shop: (1) pause its writes, the API returns a temporary error to its writes, reads go on from shared tables; (2) wait for the relay to send all its outbox rows; (3) copy rows and count each table on both sides; (4) switch the map; (5) resume writes after every Pod's map cache time.
If the row counts differ in step 3, the move stops and writes reopen in the old place.
The write pause is longer than the map cache time, so no Pod writes to the old place after the switch; the other shops do not pause at any step.
The old rows in the shared tables are deleted only after a check period, assumed one week.
The review's risks table: row counts matching while content differs is a risk; a tester is to add a checksum comparison over a few columns before the map switches.

Restoring a shop in shared tables: recover the whole server to just before the incident into a separate instance, as pitr.sh does with container db-pitr, read that shop's rows there and copy them back into donhang; other shops do not go back in time, but the copying is manual and slow.
pitr.sh recovers the server into the separate db-pitr container while db keeps running, then copies the deleted order_items rows from db-pitr back into db.
Point-in-time recovery of a PostgreSQL 17 server returns every database on that server to the same moment, so restoring in place would take every other shop back too.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 25.3 Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery

claims.text: A shop with its own database on a server of its own is restored alone from its own backup (ADR consequences: each own database has its own backup); while it shares a server with donhang, PITR covers the whole cluster, so it is restored beside.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/multi-shop-design-review.md @ stage-4 lines 71-72, 76-80; docs/adr/0026-... lines 55-56; PostgreSQL 17 docs 25.3: PITR restores only an entire database cluster

claims.text: CH-5 measure: the moving shop stops taking writes for at most 15 minutes (assumed), and other shops see no change.
A separate deployment is what ADR 0012 keeps for a contract that demands one; ADR 0026 lists a moved shop needing more isolation than a database as ADR 0012's review condition.

Trade-off rows: resuming at once risks writes in the old place via stale cached entries; no cache adds a query per request and stops every request at once if shops is unreadable; restoring in place fails driver 2.
If the cache time were raised to five minutes, each move's pause would last the time to the switch (outbox wait, copy, counts) plus five minutes and should be checked against CH-5 first.
claims.source_hint: Follows from review lines 59-62 and CH-5 measure

claims.text: The largest shop holds about 10% of orders, the level at which capacity-plan.md says the plan must be redone.
